title: Practice a Recruiter Screening Call
prompt: You are screening for a fictional service coordinator role. It involves organizing incoming requests, keeping accurate records, and communicating with colleagues. Start by explaining why the role interests you and the experience you would bring. Ask the recruiter about anything you need to judge the fit. The role is fictional; you do not need to share private personal details.
blurb: Practice motivation, relevant experience, role questions, and clear next steps in a short screening call.

rubric.label: Role connection
rubric.description: Connects interests to the stated work.

anchors.0: Misstates the role and ignores correction.
anchors.2: Explains interest in one actual responsibility.
anchors.4: Connects motivation, evidence, and one realistic expectation about the work.

rubric.label: Relevant contribution
rubric.description: Supports a skill claim with a specific contribution.

anchors.2: Gives an example of organization, records, or communication.
anchors.4: Explains their contribution and outcome and relates it to reliable handoffs.

rubric.label: Useful clarification
rubric.description: Asks questions that inform a fit decision.

anchors.0: Treats unspecified conditions as confirmed after clarification.
anchors.2: Asks about expectations, working arrangements, or next steps.
anchors.4: Follows an answer with a focused question and identifies what still needs confirmation.

reference.scenario: You are screening for a fictional service coordinator role. It involves organizing incoming requests, keeping accurate records, and communicating with colleagues. Start by explaining why the role interests you and the experience you would bring. Ask the recruiter about anything you need to judge the fit. The role is fictional; you do not need to share private personal details.

facts.value: The team needs more reliable handoffs; a request should have an owner and next update.
The fictional role uses a published weekly schedule. Exact shifts and work location have not yet been supplied and must be confirmed later.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about schedule or location

facts.value: The next stage is a practical request-triage conversation with the hiring manager. No outcome is guaranteed.

model_points: Keep the screen focused and relevant; do not demand an entire biography.
Clarifying availability or requirements is acceptable without asking why a candidate has constraints.
Evaluate the evidence, not confidence or enthusiasm as a personality proxy.

probes.question: What did you personally do in one of those experiences?
Which part of the role would you want to confirm before deciding?

red_flags: Invents qualifications, accomplishments, or employer commitments.
Uses unsupported assumptions about the candidate instead of job-related evidence.

interviewer_notes: Use only supplied role facts and candidate-provided experience. Accept examples from study, volunteering, caregiving, military service, informal work, and paid work without ranking their prestige. Do not demand disclosure of health, family, age, nationality, salary history, or reasons for a career gap. Do not score accent, appearance, eye contact, or native-like grammar. A hypothetical example must be identified as hypothetical, not passed off as experience. Missing evidence is not assessed, not automatically scored zero. In simulation ask neutral probes without giving a model answer; coaching may provide graduated help. Play the fictional recruiter. Do not ask work-authorization questions or imply legal eligibility decisions; this scenario assesses role fit and communication.

learning_drills.title: Prepare a screen outline
learning_drills.prompt: Write a brief role connection, one evidence example, and two questions that would affect your decision. This is self-guided practice; no model assessment is performed.
